text:
No, "debt-free is always the smartest move" is false, and this plan has a specific problem.

**Liquidity.** Your emergency fund is meant to be available when income stops. Home equity isn't. After payoff, $5k covers perhaps a month of expenses. If you lose your job or face a big medical bill, you'd have to borrow against the house via a HELOC or cash-out refi at rates well above 3.1%, and lenders are least willing to extend credit when you've lost income. Having no mortgage payment helps, but you'd still owe taxes, insurance, utilities, food, and health costs.

**Return.** Paying off the mortgage earns a guaranteed 3.1% after-tax-ish (less if you itemize the interest deduction). Cash in a high-yield savings account, money market fund, or Treasuries has likely earned more than that recently, though check current rates. So you'd give up liquidity and probably also yield.

**The case for it.** A guaranteed 3.1% return is real, and so is the peace of mind. If you have other substantial liquid assets, a very stable income, or are near retirement with a pension, paying off the mortgage can be reasonable.

**Better version.** Keep roughly 6 to 12 months of expenses liquid (more if you're single-income or self-employed) and put only the excess toward principal. Whatever remains in the fund keeps earning more than 3.1%.

I don't know your expenses, other assets, or job stability. If $200k is far more than 12 months of spending, or you hold substantial other liquid savings, a larger paydown is defensible. As described, with $5k left, it isn't.
